extracted.intended_audience: writers, storytellers, literary students and scholars, and readers interested in narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging whether a piece of narrative functions as Benjamin's concept of a 'story' (as distinct from information, the novel, or journalism), focusing on retellability, authority, restraint, and transmissible experience. Useful for writers and critics assessing or crafting short narratives meant for oral or memorial transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story vs. Information (durability and retellability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information 'lays claim to prompt verifiability' and is bound to its moment; a story 'preserves and concentrates its strength and is capable of releasing it even after a long time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favour narratives that endure across retellings rather than those tied to immediate facts. Anti-pattern: writing that reads like a news item or factual report — 'information dies when it is consumed.' Aim for concentrated memorable material that renews on retelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carries counsel (implicit usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true story always carries something useful — 'either a moral, a practical tip, a proverb, or a maxim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the tale provides counsel or usable wisdom, but embed it in the fabric of the tale rather than stating it overtly. Examples: proverbs, actionable tips, or moral intimations woven into events or dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woven counsel (not extracted as a lesson)
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel of a story is 'not extracted as a lesson' but is interwoven with the tale itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid explicit didacticizing or tidy moral summaries. Keep the moral/lesson emergent from the story's events and tone so listeners/readers discover it themselves rather than being lectured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storyteller as craftsman (shaping and local/depth knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The storyteller is a craftsman: either the 'settled craftsman' (deep knowledge of one place) or the 'traveling journeyman' (knowledge of distant lands); the greatest storytellers fuse both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground stories in concrete, practiced knowledge and craft. Develop sensory/local detail or worldly variety depending on storyteller type. Craft implies slow shaping and an acquired skill set rather than improvisatory reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaped slowly and polished by retelling
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is a craft object, shaped slowly, polished by retelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write and revise with an ear toward how a tale will sound when told again. Prioritize forms and phrases that survive repetition; test for lossless transmission across versions. Anti-pattern: hastily assembled anecdotes that fall apart on repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserves transmissible experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The storyteller 'takes what he tells from experience — his own or that reported by others. And he in turn makes it the experience of those who are listening to his tale.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the story carry lived, transmissible experience rather than abstract argument. Use concrete scenes, embodied detail, and reportive texture so listeners can appropriate the experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Half-art of restraint (leave gaps; avoid explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Half the art of storytelling is to keep a story free from explanation as one reproduces it.' Leave gaps and trust the listener; explanation kills the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist over-explaining motives, contexts, or meanings. Provide enough to evoke but leave interpretive space. Anti-pattern: excessive authorial exposition or neat signposting of themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfinished quality (openness to continuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story remains open — 'free of explanation,' available for continuation; the novel concludes definitively, the story invites retelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor endings and structures that feel extendable or interpretively open rather than sealed. Allow resonances that invite listeners to add, adapt, or continue the tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of the lived (death as source of authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Not only a man's knowledge or wisdom, but above all his real life... first assumes transmissible form at the moment of his death.' The dying impart authority to stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant narratives authority through their grounding in lived experience, testimony, or moments of existential weight (traditionally deathbed testimony). Avoid claims to authority based solely on rhetoric or abstract theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronicler's stance (narration without historicizing explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chronicler narrates events without distinguishing major from minor—every event is part of a larger plan; the chronicler is closer to the storyteller than the historian, who explains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a narrational stance that recounts incidents and lets pattern emerge, rather than over-analysing or subsuming events under explanatory schemata. Anti-pattern: turning a tale into a history-lesson that prioritizes causation and analysis over narrated experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context of listening (boredom and receptive conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Boredom is the dream bird that hatches the egg of experience.' A culture without spaces of receptive boredom loses the conditions for storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the audience's conditions for reception: craft stories for contexts where listeners have time and attention to dwell. Recognize that modern distraction undermines the cultural competence for storytelling; adapt form and pacing accordingly.
